tr.td: Triads, the Chinese secret-society criminal brotherhoods
Hong Kong, with branches in mainland China, Taiwan and overseas
Said to be anti-Manchu secret societies of the Qing era
14K, Sun Yee On, Wo Shing Wo and Wo Hop To
Protection rackets, gambling, vice, loan-sharking and drug dealing

li.a: BBC News: Hong Kong protests: Were triads involved in the attacks?
The Independent: Triads and China do Hong Kong deal
The New Republic: Partners in Crime, Gangs of Hong Kong
ProPublica: The Gangster Who Changed Money Laundering
Foreign Policy: Why Is Hong Kong Erupting?
Global Taiwan Institute: Taiwan's Underworld, Part 2

content.p: A triad is a Chinese criminal brotherhood built on oaths, ritual and a family-like hierarchy. The word covers many separate societies rather than one organisation. In Hong Kong, the groups BBC named as particularly notorious are the 14K, the Sun Yee On and the Wo Shing Wo. Oxford criminologist Federico Varese describes them as "very localised" groups that run protection rackets, prostitution and petty drug dealing, and says they are not international organisations.

The reporting that exists, from a 1997 magazine investigation to coverage of the street violence of 2019, shows a more tangled story. Triads began, by their own account, as rebels. They became racketeers, and in the late twentieth century they were accused of striking a bargain with the state they once claimed to oppose.

The origin story varies with the teller. The Independent wrote in 1997 that the triads began as patriotic societies opposed to rule by the Manchu Qing dynasty in the eighteenth century, and that they "quickly degenerated into criminality". The New Republic, in the same year, said the first triads were, according to legend, seventeenth-century monks set on overthrowing the Manchus, who had conquered China in 1644. By the nineteenth century, it said, the Manchus were still in power and the movement had largely turned into a criminal underground based mainly in Hong Kong and Shanghai.

Politics did not disappear from the story. The New Republic claimed that Sun Yat-sen, whose followers founded the Republic of China when the Qing fell in 1911, was himself a triad. It added that in 1927 Chiang Kai-shek, described there as another triad-turned-political-leader, used his Shanghai society, the Green Gang, against the emerging Communist Party, and that in April of that year the gang killed Communists by the hundreds. When the Communists took power in 1949, the magazine wrote, Shanghai triads fled to Hong Kong, which settled the territory as the centre of Chinese organised crime. Afterwards, with few exceptions, Hong Kong's societies professed loyalty to Taiwan and regarded the Communist Party as an ideological enemy.
Hong Kong law took aim at the societies early. According to The New Republic, simply belonging to a triad society has been illegal there since 1845.

Varese told the BBC that triads are hierarchical, with strict codes of conduct and pacts like those between blood brothers. Recruits traditionally take part in a ritual in which a chicken is beheaded and its blood dripped into a cup that is passed around, while the rules are read out. Recruits tend to be naked or half-naked, he said, because the idea is to forget a previous identity and join a made-up family of brothers. Most members are working class and have little higher education, and many join young, recruited from their own neighbourhood. "Once you're in, you could be there for all your life," he said, although some become dormant members and go into business.

The New Republic added colour from a 1980s trial. A Sun Yee On enforcer, called a Red Pole, told a court he had been inducted in 1981 in a ceremony led by an official in a Taoist monk's robe holding a wooden sword. Twelve recruits lined up against an altar and drank "red flower wine", which the witness said combined wine with their own blood and that of a freshly beheaded chicken.

The same magazine described the societies as less tightly organised than Mafia families. In its account, membership offered solidarity, easy access to criminal partners and the implied threat of brothers ready to hurt people. It said triad brutality was often marked by the cleaver, or "chopper". It also wrote that women cannot be triads and that boys as young as 10 were recruited by the major societies, a different picture from Varese's account of mostly working-class members who join young.

Nobody gives a firm figure, and the estimates are far apart. The Independent said in 1997 that about 30,000 triad members were said to operate in Hong Kong. The New Republic put the Sun Yee On alone at no fewer than 30,000 and possibly 60,000, and noted that the low figure exceeded the size of the Hong Kong Police Force. The BBC, in 2019, cited a 2017 South China Morning Post estimate of as many as 100,000 members in a city of 7.3 million people.

The police figures count crimes, not members. In 2018 the Hong Kong Police Force recorded 1,715 triad-related crimes, according to the BBC. The bulk were assaults and woundings, and some were clashes between rival groups.

One prosecution shows both the reach of the societies and the limits of the law. The New Republic reported that in February 1986 Anthony Chung, a former policeman who had become a Red Pole of the Sun Yee On, turned himself in and asked for protection after a gambling-debt quarrel with another Red Pole. He became an undercover informant. Chung claimed to have dealt with the society's "Dragon Head", or boss, whom he named as Heung Wah-yim, eldest son of Heung Chin, who had founded the Sun Yee On in 1919.

On 1 April 1987, the magazine wrote, officers led by Chief Superintendent Brian Merritt arrested eleven suspected members, Heung among them. In a filing cabinet at the law office where Heung worked, police found a list of roughly 900 numbered names that looked like a roster of Sun Yee On office-bearers. The trial that followed was billed as the biggest organised-crime trial in Hong Kong's history, with Heung and five others in the dock. Five other suspects had pleaded guilty.

Heung took the stand and told the court he was the president of a local Lions Club chapter and that the list was of prospective donors to Chinese festivals. On 20 January 1988, after one day of deliberation, the jury convicted Heung, his son, his son-in-law and two others of triad-related offences and acquitted the sixth defendant. Heung was sentenced to seven and a half years.

It did not hold. On 13 December 1989 the chief justice, Sir Ti-liang Yang, ruled that the name list had been wrongly admitted because the prosecution's expert witnesses were not qualified to authenticate it. He also held that the two Red Poles, being accomplices in the same alleged crimes, could not back each other up. The verdict was quashed and Heung walked free, saying "Justice is fair". The prosecutor, Kevin Egan, told the magazine he regarded the ruling as a "hometown verdict" and later left the Crown to become a defence lawyer who represents accused Sun Yee On members. Those are Egan's words and opinions, not a finding of any court.

The most consequential claim about the triads concerns the run-up to the 1997 handover of Hong Kong. In May 1997 Wong Man-fong, a former deputy secretary-general of the Hong Kong branch of the New China News Agency, told an academic forum that he had met triad leaders "to befriend" them before the handover agreement. The Independent quoted him saying he told them the administration wanted a peaceful return and they must not upset Hong Kong's prosperity and stability. In return, the paper reported, China pledged to turn a blind eye to their activities. The New Republic quoted him differently: "if they did not disrupt Hong Kong's stability, we would not stop them from making money".

The paper said that China's problem was the Sun Yee On, which had been close to anti-Communist Taiwan. In late 1984, it reported, Xu Jiatun, head of the news agency, invited the Sun Yee On "dragon heads" to meetings where something akin to a peace pact was signed. The other big societies, the 14K and Wo On Lok, were more co-operative from the start. The Independent also noted that Deng Xiaoping said in 1984 that there were "many good guys" among the triads, and that China's security minister had spoken of "patriotic elements" among them.

The New Republic went further than the other accounts. It argued that the arrangement would "seal what amounts to a cooperation pact" between triads and the Communist Party, and claimed that the Sun Yee On no longer required initiates to pledge loyalty to Taiwan but to the People's Republic. It alleged triad ventures with mainland institutions in nightclubs, karaoke bars and brothels, and quoted Tao Siju, then head of the Public Security Bureau, saying in April 1993 that triads who were patriotic and concerned for Hong Kong's stability should be united with. Those are the magazine's allegations and quotations, not rulings of any court, and the Chinese authorities are not quoted denying them in the pages reviewed here.

The magazine also profiled the businessman Albert Yeung, who denied being a triad. In 1994 he was arrested and charged with criminal intimidation and false imprisonment after a dispute with a former currency trader. At trial in May the next year, according to the magazine, the witnesses said they were afraid or could no longer remember the incident, and the judge dismissed the charges, saying "I cannot be sure justice has been done." Yeung called the accusation of triad membership a product of jealousy. Charles Heung, a son of the Sun Yee On's founder, also appears in the account. The magazine said a 1992 US Senate subcommittee had named him among the society's top office-bearers. He told the magazine his family had "a Mafia background" but that he personally knew little of such matters.

The New Republic challenged the idea that triads harm only each other. In January 1997, it wrote, young Sun Yee On members and young Wo Shing Wo members had a territorial dispute and firebombed a karaoke club in Kowloon; seventeen people died. It also described the 1996 attack on a magazine publisher, Leung Tin-wai, whose left forearm was cut off with a chopper two days before his publication launched. The magazine said the debut issue came out on schedule without a triad-related article.

Allegations that triads can be hired as political muscle returned during the pro-democracy protests. In 2014, when tens of thousands occupied Hong Kong's streets, violence erupted at the Mong Kok protest site as attackers beat protesters and tore down tents and barriers. Police said 19 of those arrested had triad backgrounds, the BBC reported. Varese and Rebecca Wong of City University of Hong Kong studied the attacks through eyewitnesses and two people with triad links, one a senior member. They concluded that the attackers belonged to triads from outside Mong Kok and had been paid, while some local triads opposed the attack as an encroachment on their territory. Their informants suggested "business interests" that wanted to impress the Chinese government had paid. The legislator James To accused the government of using "organised, orchestrated forces and even triad gangs". The government and police denied colluding with triads, and one police commander called the claim "ridiculous".

In July 2019, according to the BBC, dozens of masked men with wooden sticks and metal rods stormed a train station in Hong Kong and assaulted people returning from a protest, along with passers-by. The attack left 45 people injured. The BBC said there was widespread speculation that the attackers were triads and that police sources told the South China Morning Post they believed members of the 14K and Wo Shing Wo were among them. That was the paper's sourcing; the BBC did not itself confirm the identities. Varese called it a "carbon copy" of 2014, only more serious because passers-by were hit, and said the aim looked like frightening people rather than killing them.

Protesters and pro-democracy legislators accused police of arriving only after the attackers had left. The police chief called that suggestion a "smear", saying the force was stretched by violent protests elsewhere. Foreign Policy listed the alleged collusion of police with triad attackers among the reasons for the anger on the streets, and warned that deniable forces such as triads might be used again. The authorities have rejected the claims of collusion.

Elsewhere in the region the same pattern, a gangster class living in the shadow of a political authority, is reported on a larger scale. The Global Taiwan Institute wrote in 2024 that Taiwan's gangs found a permissive environment in mainland China after crackdowns in the 1980s and 1990s. It cited the account of the scholar Ko-Lin Chin that local Communist Party officials did not see Taiwanese gangsters as a threat to public order as long as they avoided serious crime on the mainland, and that crimes aimed at Taiwan were tolerated. The institute described Chang An-lo, an early leader of the Bamboo Union, who the institute says lived in Shenzhen as a fugitive from 1996 to 2013. It said he registered a political party in Taiwan after returning in 2013, and that the party is widely suspected to be a front for the gang. These are the institute's assessments. The Bamboo Union is a Taiwanese gang, not a Hong Kong triad.

ProPublica's 2022 investigation described a different branch of Chinese organised crime. It reported that US Drug Enforcement Administration agents identified a Chinese American launderer, Xizhi Li, whose couriers collected cartel cash in Chicago's Chinatown. According to court records cited by ProPublica, Li pleaded guilty and received a 15-year sentence. Adm. Craig Faller told Congress that Chinese launderers had emerged as the "No. 1 underwriter" of drug trafficking in the Western Hemisphere and that the Chinese government was "at least tacitly supporting" the laundering; some other US officials went further. ProPublica said such state complicity is difficult to prove, and Beijing rejects the accusation. It did not describe Li as a triad member.
content.h2: What is established, and what is not
content.p: Several things are on firm ground. Triad societies exist, the law has treated membership as an offence for well over a century, and police data record triad-related violence every year. A jury convicted Sun Yee On office-bearers in 1988, and the Heung case shows how hard the evidence is to build and to defend on appeal.

Others rest on single sources or on allegation: the handover bargain described by one former official in 1997, the claim that triads were paid to attack protesters in 2014 and 2019, and the suggestion of police complicity. Each has been disputed by the people it implicates.
